top_comments.author: @adamofblastworks1517
top_comments.text: This makes me feel bittersweet, like remembering good times that you must remember, but are about to end or already have.This makes me think about things like high school ending in a few months and no longer seeing certain people anymore; my grandmother might not be around much longer; several good friends that I have completely lost or nearly lost total contact with abruptly. It makes me happy, nostalgic, and sad (not quiet depressed) at the same time. But this is good. It is good to remember these things, and remember to enjoy life, make good memories, and spend time with the people you love. It is good to reminisce every once in a while, to make sure that you haven't forgotten what is important, and to make sure that you are living your life like you want to.

top_comments.author: @simplygarza8511
top_comments.text:
Hey Martin... I know this comment will be lost in the sea. But I just wanted to say... Thank you.

This song is by far my favorite other than the iconic Marble Machine song. I've been a sub ever since that video was uploaded. I was still in high school, a couple anxious months of graduating.

Well, now I have since graduated. 2016 was a big year for me in so many ways. So much has changed since then. The friends I once was so close with have all started lives of their own. The girl I used to love and be with broke up with me. But now, we're still close, and she's even a Cadet at West Point. I had been enlisted and finally graduated AIT and went to my first unit then. 

Now, I'm almost done with my contract. I have a new girlfriend that I used to go to school with and have known for years, a steady job and I'm about to pick up a new one. The future is looking bright for me so far.

But this song... It brings me back to simpler times. When my biggest worry was finishing an essay on time 😂 It makes me happy to reminisce on such simple times. It makes me miss them, but at the same time, they shaped me to who I am today. It's such a bittersweet song because it makes me excited to explor

I took 10 years of classical piano lessons.  I used to be able to play 18 page sonatas with my eyes closed.  Some traumatic things happened, my beautiful grand piano was taken away from me and sold... and I couldn't bear to play piano again after that.  Every time I listened to someone playing it, it would make me cry.

Today, seeing this - I finally want to sit down at the little upright piano I now have, and find my way back to music.   This will be the first thing I learn in two decades.   Thank you, beautiful people of Wintergatan.  You inspire me more than you could ever know.

top_comments.author: @lillyrichter3383
top_comments.text:
Wow, I’ve got so many things to say!

First of all: This "vlog" is a beautiful video itself. It’s not just you informing us about the future of Wintergatan, it’s also a poem, a tutorial on how to sew, a wonderfully depicted  allegory of your upcoming plans with the solar system and much more. You put so much effort into making a cool green screen, filming and into editing, it’s so enjoyable to watch!

Secondly, I’m so excited about everything that is to come. The new album, the new marble machine, the tour, the mideos ... you are doing so many cool things! You are a huge inspiration and motivation for me to stop being lazy and do something myself.

Finally, I wanted to say that I’d love to watch new mideos on a weekly basis, but don’t overextend yourself. I know you have the creativity, talent and energy of eleven men and three young horses, but I know myself how hard it can be to stick to a tight schedule with producing videos. You might get into a hurry and make yourself too much pressure, and when that happens you might stop enjoying recording and editing them, and that would be sad. 

So if you have to deal with unnecessary stress to keep up with the weekly mideos, just go easy

top_comments.author: @slaeshjag
top_comments.text:
A story about doors:

A lab at my uni was shutting down. As a result, a laser cutter had to go. They just wanted it to disappear. It was too big to fit through the door, so the plan was to take it to bits and junk it, which was a shame, since it was fully working. Meanwhile, a professor at this university was trying to put together a mentorspace (a makerspace that doesn't suck, essentially), and a lasercutter was something it could really use. The whole thing with it not fitting through the door was troublesome, and if it was taken to bits, who knows if it would ever work again. So this professor called up the right people and asked a very innocent question: "how much would it cost to repair a wall?". The reply he got back was "about 5000 SEK". Within 5 minutes, they were tearing down the wall.

This laser cutter is now the most used piece of equipment in the lab.

Welcome to the Design Discussion,
Maybe this could be a good place to have a public discussion and for me to receive all your feedback, could maybe be a returning thing in this series, lets try!

So first of all, please keep this clean and about the design, its the constructive criticism we are really looking for here.
I tried to give enough background information in the video to explain the situation
Consider this important fact: there is 15.000 holes/places for pins on the MMX per programming setup (30.000 if we make two setups)  any suggestion involving manual operations multiplied by 30.000 is nearly impossible. (if one manual operation takes 1 minute, 30.000 is a couple of months straight work. We need an automated solution.)
We need a very accurate solution for the musical timing.
It need to be FAST and EASY to reprogram. 

I would love to hear what you think about my last proposed idea or a completely different solution i didn’t think of.

Thanks a lot/ Martin

videos.title: Is Fusion 360 Unable to Handle Large Assemblies? - Marble Machine X #31

top_comments.author: @kitingmare
top_comments.text: For those wondering. The issue with the large assemblies described here is mostly a CPU bottleneck (especially since solving geometry is really hard to parallelize and runs mostly on one core). A better CPU only improves things marginally (there is no 20Ghz processor core as far as I know...). The way Martin explains, is to optimize the assembly for performance and eliminating individual solving bottlenecks by avoiding some commands and/or using them in a specific manner. Another issue that can appear is a GPU bottleneck which is mostly due to complicated appearances like the 3D wood appearance. By using relatively basic visuals while designing this bottleneck can easily be minimized. The other way is to throw better hardware at the problem. But seeing the same problem on my PC as on Martin's MacBook seems to show that you would have to throw a LOT of power at it...

top_comments.author: @MichaelAlm
top_comments.text: Acrylic can be challenging. The heat gun isn't going to yield consistent bends. The jig is also drawing the heat away. I recommend a strip heater. They also make heat pads you can lay on the acrylic to make a very nice gentle bend. These options will help provide constant heat over the whole surface. Hope that helps and good luck!! the MMX is looking fantastic!!

top_comments.author: @Wintergatan

top_comments.author: @ethanhermsey
top_comments.text:
Hey listen, I did an internship at a plastic/acrylic shop. 
The heatgun technique is only good for a 'line' bend. The compound bend you are trying to achieve is too much. You would want to heat the whole sheet evenly.

Find a big oven (maybe one of the local baguette bakers would want to help you? ;p ) 
Don't clamp the sheet to the mold, it will form on its own with the help of gravity. Make sure the gaps in the mold are not too big or the material will droop in the holes.
Set the oven to 160 degrees Celsius and within minutes the material will start to bend. Don't let it cool down too fast. 

I hope this might help you. Good luck, the machine is looking good :D

Latest News: Maybe we did find an alternative programming wheel design yesterday, brainstorming with the team! (after the recording of this video) 

As I mention inside the video the most popular suggestion for a design change is to have the songs preprogrammed on tour. This would only be practical if the sections are redesigned into something much smaller and lighter. 
Yesterday I talked about pop rivets in a thin metal sheet with holes drilled by the CNC machine and then Tim Keller mentioned a welding stud gun and that we could bolt one to my cnc machine then I found this:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SzLPZj_lkwk
a welding stud gun CNC machine from HBS, Germany, 
The idea here is to use thin metal sheet and have the CNC machine accurately weld on the programming pins to the flat sheet.
The sheet is thin enough to easily bend around the radius of the programming wheel.
To save weight you could laser cut the sheets beforehand and remove a lot of excessive material.
The songs could be transported flat, and perhaps even be cut in one length, although 267 cm is probably to large surface to cover for the machine so maybe two halves is the practical choice.

top_comments.author: @Wintergatan
top_comments.text:
The Marble Conveyer Belt is Completed and it delivers.
- lifts 8 marbles per crank turn.
- thanks to it being driven by ratchets and pistons, it makes a short halt to load and unload the marbles, on exactly the same spot every time.
- The pistons are connected to the crank shaft with a 2:1 gear reduction which means that the conveyer belt go in time with the music, and in half time. I can even use the mechanical sounds from the ratchets and the marbles climbing the fish stair to create parts of the beats.
- I only had one kick drum channel up and running so the kick drum plays on 2-4 like a snare normally would. Sounds a little strange but I just made this piece of music to demonstrate the concepts are working. (no music you hear in the videos are going to be used for the album, its quick and dirty functional pieces for the videos only)
- Its been a journey but we are now on our way. Again.
- the throw of the pistons s 40mm, the pitch of the chain is 15,875x2 mm, an imperial value, and it happens to be exactly twice the marble diameter. All this makes it possible to lift exactly one row of marbles per crank turn. The ratchets move 40 mm but only grabs onto the chain to move it exac

top_comments.author: @Wintergatan
top_comments.text:
When I was a kid we used to go visit my grandmother and grandfather and they had an old Treadle pedaled Singer sewing machine. I could sit for hours just pedaling that machine, I was totally in awe over how it's flywheel transformed the up and down motion of the treadle pedal into a rotating motion. When I was sketching the design for the Marble Machine X that childhood memory struck me like a bolt and I knew I had to incorporate something similar into the MMX and now it is finally completed! 


It took some iterations to find the correct geometry, to have the correct motion but now I would say it works perfect. The pedal is connected to a CAM shaft on the crank shaft and it moves in time with the music. Every downstroke of the pedal is like a metronome click to the songs which allows me to basically tap the beat of the song and play music instruments with two hands. It also gives some rest for the arms :).


By the way: I listened back to last weeks snare sound, it sounds pretty awful :). haha, will be follow up videos on me fixing that sound, we need CRISP. C R I S P.
 
HUGE Thanks to everyone who are watching and supporting this looong Marble Machine X Project! 
Good luck with y

top_comments.author: @tahantomusic8904
top_comments.text:
I think you might be overthinking this and making it more difficult for yourself. 
There is one factor that you need to keep in mind for future testing and that is that you are not testing with the resonator pipes. Those are designed to amplify the desired overtones of the bars when they are being struck. (It's like testing a guitar tone without its body.)  I just tested out various points on the Vibraphone in the band room and I had difficulty hearing what I was hearing in the video.  Yes you are supposed to hit at about halfway between the center and where the string attaches for the best sound. But you need to have resonator pipes too. 
That with the dampening liquid latex, you might find that you can find a consistent place among all the bars. 


And speaking of resonator pipes, have you thought about having tunable resonator pipes like organ pipes? 
Might make changing notes easier because you wouldn't need to have a different pipe for each bar. You could have marked locations on the adjustable pipes that you set the adjuster to and lock it in place.

top_comments.text:
MMX has to work when repeatedly disassembled and transported around the world, in Rain, in Wind, in Warm and Cool and Humid conditions. MMX is a confluence of metal, wood, plastic, and other materials. And yet so many components are built to a tolerance of 0.1mm and if that tolerance is off, all joy stops. Many times throughout the build, I've seen designs implemented where the tolerance, temperature, and humidity are in a strictly controlled situation and it works. But if any of those variables change, disaster!

I'm a huge fan and have been trying to think of constructive ways to express my increasing concerns without coming off as a jerk.  I believe in the project and am a supporter. But there are a lot of potentially temperamental aspects here that there's almost a certainty will fail under tour conditions. You've got the MMX to a very close completion and I think it can be absolutely saved. But to do it, I think some things will be simplified and stripped away, and some other ways to interface disparate materials other than having a 0.1mm tolerance will have to be found.

top_comments.author: @WhatAboutTheBee
top_comments.text: 20:43 "Hopefully I don't have to revisit this".  Sadly, yes you will Martin.  The issue is called "Chain Stretch".  Chain stretch is when your metal chain elongates.  How does it do that?  The chain links are connected with a two pins, usually one solid pin rotating inside the other hollow pin.  They rub and wear against each other.  Each link only contributes a small amount of wear, but in aggregate, it is significant contribution to chain elongation.  The solution is NOT a fixed sprocket location, pinned mechanically as you have done.  Either provide a spring loaded idler or spring load an axle that holds the sprocket.  Also, plan on replacing the chain periodically, as it will wear out.  Yes, you will re-visit this issue again. :(

top_comments.text:
There is always going to be a tradeoff between dissipating pressure from the marble stack and the risk of them getting stuck. If _all_ the pressure is being dissipated off to the sides, then effectively the marbles are being _held_ in place against the walls, and getting stuck. The ideal design would be one that dissipates just enough pressure to allow the gates to operate, but not so much that marbles can get jammed inside.

TBH, I think in practice this sort of sticking is going to be a lot less common than in the test setup though, because the whole machine is vibrating, the gates are slamming in and out just under the pressure tracks, there's a lot more 'noise' to jiggle the marbles and keep them moving.

top_comments.text:
Warning! Large diameter gears for toothed belts are surprisingly difficult! I speak from experience here. The reason is this:

When you mesh a small gear with a big gear you are only engaging the big gear over a tiny fraction of the overall circumference. This means that tiny imperfections in the pitch of the gear teeth don't matter. However, when you mesh a toothed belt with a big gear, any tiny pitch imperfection will be multiplied by over 50% of the enormous circumference! The belt will pass in and out of phase with the gear teeth, resulting in slipping and sadness. Also, if the belt stretches at all when you tension it or as it ages, the pitch will change, and a gear that used to be good will now be bad.

This is a large risk in your new design! If you want to go down this road, rigorously test these gears FIRST so you know what you're getting into and can change course if you need to before it's too late!

top_comments.text: Martin, once you reach the correct geometry, you should learn from the past when you didn't damp any of the contacts in your mechanical parts. All of the small contacts are individually not very loud, but it adds up quickly. So you should always account for a small layer of damping (thin elastomer, felt lining, or bounceless combination thereof) wherever two hard components come into a momentary shock. It's not possible everywhere but just look at the details of a high quality piano action (Renner) : There are lots of dampers everywhere, from tiny rubber discs to large felt bands. Another thing that piano actions can teach you, is that some distances need to be adjustable — piano actions have a capstan-like device to raise or lower the hammers precisely ; as well, the escapement mechanism is adjustable. The reason for all this, is that mechanical parts (even in metal) undergo dimensional changes over time and over variations in temperature/humidity. If you want truly inert parts the only solution would be high performance ceramics (carbides) but that is costly and nearly impossible to machine. As an avid cyclist, here's two pieces of advice in using these cables:
1) Get the expensive stuff. It's MUCH more durable when it comes to rust, kinks, stretching cables, and glide friction. Cheaper cables will eventually betray you in exceptionally frustrating ways.
2) Use the endcaps (ferrules) that come with the cable. They prevent the outer wire from fraying, and stop dust and grime being funneled into the channel on every actuation.

Edit with more ideas from the replies:
3) Do not push on these cables. It'll work for a while, but eventually your cable will buckle. Instead, make sure the inner cable is always under tension. The mute mechanism will fail in this regard, the marble dropper gets it right.
4) Cable stretch will introduce timing errors. You won't measure this in the studio or your tests now, but you'll absolutely know before the end of your world tour. Maybe not introduce this vulnerability into the dropper design? Alternatively, get the good stuff and have adjustments like on a bike.

top_comments.author: @andyjbauman
top_comments.text:
12:04:  If you are using that light green disc as a brake, ensure you review the following:
1. The material needs to be an actual friction material, metal-to-metal contact will cause galling.
2. The flat head bolts need to sub-flush of the green disc.
3. The bolts connecting the thicker green disc need to be stiff enough to resist the torque being applied.  Bolts are really not designed to bend, which is how you are loading them in this application.
4.  The material of the 'brake disc' needs to be thick and stiff enough that it does not turn into a cone when you apply a load axially. The same applies to the pink ring to which the bowden tubes are connected.
5.  The two hex nuts between the green disc and the cyan disc would need to be set very accurately to ensure those two plates are perpendicular with the axis of rotation.  You many want to replace those two hex nuts with a machined sleeve that can slip over the bolt and accurately set that distance.

Hi Martin!

At around 4:30, you talked about reaming. As a machinist (or soon-to-be, I'm still at school), I would tell you that the hole that you plan on cutting at 19.9 millimeters, I would resize them at 19.5 millimeters. If you plan on using a machine (a press drill, hand drill, or a milling machine), I'll give you the equation to calculate the spindle speed :

(90 (the Surface feet per minute, or SFM for short, of steel) * 1000) / (pi * tool diameter) = Machine RPM
Then, divide all this by 4 because you're reaming (it puts a lot of stress on the tool). Also, make sure you're using A LOT of cutting oil, because reamers tend to generate a lot of heat.
In this case, ((90*1000)/(3.1416*20))/4 equals 358 RPM.

Why am I telling you all of this? Because I don't think hand reaming in your situation is doing you any good. You cannot, and I repeat, cannot drill, ream, or even tap by hand being 100% straight, it's impossible. top_comments.author: @apersaudcv
top_comments.text: A correction; "Moment of Inertia" is the angle equivalent of mass. By increasing the angular speed, you are increasing the angular momentum of the wheel. You get L=Iw where I is moment of inertia, w is angular speed, and L is angular momentum; higher speed or moment means more momentum. More moment of inertia does = tighter because the "mass" is higher, and this means that the same force (friction) results in a smaller change in speed (loss of speed). This also means its harder to turn. You can also increase the speed to increase its momentum which has the same effect.

top_comments.text: Calculating precision in milliseconds is bringing in some confusion here, as you end up making it looking more precise at higher speeds. You have to remember that the intervals get smaller and smaller as you increase the speed. Imagine a full rotation at a given tempo being 1 ms as an example. The deviation will always be less than 1 ms, however it might still be deviating 50% off the optimal speed. You need to figure out how precisely it’s hitting the same spot relative to the speed of the full rotation. This means a percentage deviation of the full rotation. This will become apparent since the deviations will scale with the gearbox. This will essentially be re-introducing more deviation (in milliseconds) at lower speeds.

top_comments.author: @speedy3749
top_comments.text: What you missed (or didn't mention) was, that there are diminishing returns. Look at your results: 2x1.41=2.82 > 2.37 .  This means that in absolute terms, yes it is tighter. But the gain is not linear, it has diminishing returns. So you might find a point where working on the tolerances or increasing the spring strength (make the mechanisms more snappy and settle faster) might have more of an impact than pure programming wheel speed. on the other hand, lessening the spring strenght might reduce the drag on the programming wheel (it will flex in itself and the gears if it has to exert power, that might lead to increased tolerances that you can't see while the parts are not running if you look only at the machining), so there might be another tradeoff that is worth looking at.

top_comments.author: @EDLEXUS
top_comments.text:
not to dismiss the positive side effects, but there are also some important negative side effects:
1) more moment of inertia means you need better safety systems, because the danger scales similar to moment of inertia. This will be a big problem, especially when trying to find venues that would host wintergatan + machine
2) more moment of inertia means more vibrations if the flywheel is not running perfectly true. Especially on tour, big mechanical things get bumped and slightly deformend, so this is something that will only truly be visible after some time. Those vibrations are especially dangerous for shows outside of full time music halls with a solid floor. Festivals/mobile stages build their stage surface out of stagedecks/scaffholding, that is very durable for heavy compression loads, but suseptible to vibrations/dynamic loads.

I think it is important to have these things in mind when designing, because with the current plan, it looks like you are building a machine that might be able to play music, but can never leave your show, because no music venue can/wants to handle it

top_comments.author: @GruPnijla
top_comments.text:
Hi, mechanical engineer here, and I have to tell you about the problem with carbon fiber reinforced thermoplastics in gear tooth applications. I was the calculation engineer for a project where we had problems with gear strength for a gearbox with plastic gears (car seat gearbox). The gears would break all the time, so we had some carbon fiber reinforced PA CF30 (Polyamid with 30% Carbon Fibre) gears made. The problem with gear teeth breaking went away instantly, but the downside was tat the wear of the plastic gear flanks exposed the underlying carbon fibers. Those turned the otherwise smooth gear flank surfaces into wire brushes with microscopic carbon wires sticking out, which very rapidly caused the bronze gear from the electric motor to wear down in no time.
We hat to switch that over to steel to get over the required lifetime, which made the gearbox too loud. In the end we found a few mm more width for the gears and stayed with non-reinforced PA and bronze.
So if you find that your gear flanks are wearing out too fast, consider switching back to non-reinforced material at least for the tooth carrier parts. For geometric long-term stability of non-sliding parts the CF-reiinfor

Trouble with design requirements is that it's really a tool for a team of people, to stop the design shooting off in random directions at the whim of the individuals.
It's an agreement. But in this case, it's an agreement with yourself.
Problem is, if you ALWAYS reserve the right to change the requirements for your artistic needs, it's kinda pointless, you're just writing a commentary on the development of your design.
If you NEVER allow yourself to change the requirements, then you will feel restricted and frustrated and likely shelve the project.
So, if you are going to use this, you need to be clear with yourself about which elements are your "Bible" and which elements are your "suggestions".

Hey Martin, I would like to give you an advice for something you keep struggling. Don't bang your head against the wall by forcing yourself doing a massive design requirements document that you will never use. You are an artist. I am an engineer and we create massive design requirement documents for huge projects with hundreds of people involved, where it's about a lot of money. You on the other hand are 1 person.

Layer 3: How to archive layer 2? How to transport X marbles per minute back up. Give yourself a few options: 5/10/15 marbles per row -> this gives you different speeds of the axis.

The reason I mentioned the TODO list, is because it introduces a very clear time axis, in contrast to "design requirements" that are timeless. There is no time dimension in design requirements, just a list of "what you want" at some point in the future. But the problem with that is that you don´t completley know that before you start the project, because it depends on how long it takes to make each component, which is an unknown. This is a core principle of Agile software development, used also on hardware by companies such as Space X. Instead of writing a list of requirements, make a list of steps to improve something, and prioritize what is most important (order, time). Deliver something fast, and then iterate, go back and improve. That way, when time is up and you need to deliver, you have something at least!  Note also that a plan is also not set in stone. It needs to constantly evolve and update according to the latest information.

I think the DR can include WANTS as well as NEEDS. You have to be aware of scope creep and clearly indicate it's a WANT, but you can also include it as a strong want IF POSSIBLE. The IF POSSIBLE should come with some thought out limitations, like far am I going to go to explore the idea before I cut my losses?

top_comments.author: @Thomas_de_Meijer
top_comments.text: It seems that Martin has some difficulty making a distinction between requirements and verification. I would suggest rethinking it as requirements and quantify. For example, rather than saying the machine has a certain range, the requirement becomes “the machine has enough range to produce nice music or something”. Then the specific scales it needs goes into quantify. It sounds counterintuitive but unless there is a very specific reason to have a specific value, it shouldn’t be written into the requirements. This allows you to reach conclusions based on multiple requirements. For example, an additional requirement could be “no programming between songs”. Then in combination, the range of notes you need on the machine is narrowed down to a specific set that achieves both sets of requirements.

top_comments.text:
We design medical devices, which have regulatory reasons to do all of this requirement capture. 

A tip from our quality management system
Don't just number your requirements (and when you do, simply give them an id tag like REQ-123), also name them hierachically 

REQ-1 Music: The machine shall play music
REQ-2 Music.Programmable: The music shall be programmable by the user
REC-3 Music.Instrument: The machine shall include instruments which can be played 
REQ-4 Music.Instrument.Vibraphone: The instruments shall include a vibraphone
REQ-5 Dimensions: The machine shall be limited in size
REQ-6 Dimensions.Height: The machine shall be no higher than 2m (the height of my studio)
REQ-7 Weight: The machine shall be limited in weight
REQ-8 Weight.Moveable: The machine shall be able to be moved on my pump truck 
REQ-9 Weight.Moveable.Limit: The machine shall not exceed the weight limits set by <insert pumptruck specs here>


Doing it in this tree format makes it clear that the child requirements are related to their parents, and makes it much easier to glance over them and see what is covered without having to look at a long requirement description.

Good luck Martin, hope this helps!

Design requirements are problem statements. Together they form subproblems.

top_comments.author: @isaacdnew
top_comments.text:
Mechanical engineer here. What you're calling "fatigue" is actually called creep. Creep will always have an effect on plastic parts that are subjected to constant, long-term forces. Your bistable mechanism solution would only avoid creep if it was loose in the locked state. With your proposed bistable mechanism design, the part will eventually end up with a divet in the place where the lever pushes against the wall. This will leave you with the same loss of locking force as the plastic print-in-place spring. If you want to avoid creep while maintaining a constant long-term force, the only option is to use a material that doesn't creep.

I'd suggest modifying your spring-based design to replace the plastic spring with a slot that accepts a metal compression spring. If you make sure the design keeps the spring from ever popping out, it'll be really reliable. Using a metal spring should only add a 5-second step to the manufacturing process - which I understand is significant given the number of programming profiles you'll need - but I think the reliability will be worth it.
